Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.full_text: Abstract Host classification from viral genomic sequences is challenging because biologically meaningful signals must be extracted from high-dimensional sequence data under strong class imbalance. This paper presents a hybrid quantum machine learning framework for binary human versus non-human host classification. Raw nucleotide sequences are first encoded using a frozen DNABERT-2 model and compressed into bounded low-dimensional latent vectors through a bottleneck autoencoder. These quantum-compatible features are then classified using the proposed Segment-Aware Entangled Quantum Classifier (SEQC), a compact variational quantum decision module with trainable dual-angle encoding, data re-uploading, segment-aware local-to-global entanglement, global mixing, and trainable observable readout. Experiments are conducted in a leakage-safe, resource-controlled simulation setting: classifier training uses a balanced subset of samples, while validation, threshold tuning, and testing are performed on the full natural imbalanced splits. On the natural test set, SEQC achieves \(0.8833\) accuracy, \(0.7224\) balanced accuracy, \(0.7243\) macro-F1, \(0.7740\) ROC-AUC, and \(0.5167\) minority-class PR-AUC using only \(138\) trainable classifier parameters. Comparisons with classical baselines show that SEQC is competitive as a compact nonlinear decision module, particularly in minority-class ranking. Ablation studies further indicate that encoding choice, bottleneck dimension, and entanglement structure should be matched to the supplied latent representation. analysis.background: Host classification from viral genomic sequences is difficult because biologically meaningful signals must be extracted from high‑dimensional data under strong class imbalance (F1).
analysis.methods: The authors built a hybrid quantum machine‑learning pipeline (F2) that encodes raw nucleotide sequences with a frozen DNABERT‑2 model and compresses them via a bottleneck autoencoder (F3); the resulting low‑dimensional vectors are classified by the Segment‑Aware Entangled Quantum Classifier, a variational quantum decision module with dual‑angle encoding, data re‑uploading, segment‑aware entanglement and trainable readout (F4); experiments were run in a leakage‑safe, resource‑controlled simulation where training used a balanced subset and validation/threshold tuning and testing used the full natural imbalanced splits (F5).
analysis.results: On the natural test set, SEQC achieved 0.8833 accuracy, 0.7224 balanced accuracy, 0.7243 macro‑F1, 0.7740 ROC‑AUC and 0.5167 minority‑class PR‑AUC with only 138 trainable parameters (F6).
analysis.contribution: Compared with classical baselines, SEQC is competitive as a compact nonlinear decision module, especially improving minority‑class ranking (F7).
analysis.limitations: The study was performed only in simulation (no real quantum hardware) and the paper provides only abstract‑level details, limiting assessment of real‑world applicability (F5).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Host classification from viral genomes is challenging due to high dimensionality and class imbalance (F1). Methods: A hybrid quantum ML pipeline encodes sequences with DNABERT‑2, compresses them via a bottleneck autoencoder, and classifies them with a Segment‑Aware Entangled Quantum Classifier; training used a balanced subset and testing used the full imbalanced set in a safe simulation (F2‑F5). Results: On the natural test set SEQC reached 0.8833 accuracy, 0.7224 balanced accuracy, 0.7243 macro‑F1, 0.7740 ROC‑AUC and 0.5167 minority‑class PR‑AUC with 138 parameters (F6). Contribution: SEQC performed competitively with classical baselines, notably improving minority‑class ranking (F7). Limitations: Only simulated experiments and abstract‑level reporting restrict conclusions about real‑world performance (F5).

analysis_zh.background: 从病毒基因组序列进行宿主分类困难,因为必须在强类别不平衡的高维数据中提取生物学意义的信号 (F1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者构建了一个混合量子机器学习流水线 (F2),使用冻结的 DNABERT‐2 模型对原始核苷酸序列进行编码,并通过瓶颈自编码器 (F3) 进行压缩;得到的低维向量由段感知纠缠量子分类器进行分类,该分类器是具备双角度编码、数据重新上传、段感知纠缠和可训练读出层的变分量子决策模块 (F4);实验在泄漏安全、资源受控的模拟环境中进行,训练使用平衡子集,验证/阈值调优和测试使用完整的自然不平衡划分 (F5)。
analysis_zh.results: 在自然测试集上,SEQC 以仅 138 个可训练参数实现了 0.8833 的准确率、0.7224 的平衡准确率、0.7243 的宏 F1、0.7740 的 ROC‐AUC 和 0.5167 的少数类 PR‐AUC (F6)。
analysis_zh.contribution: 与经典基线相比,SEQC 作为紧凑的非线性决策模块具有竞争力,尤其提升了少数类排序性能 (F7)。
analysis_zh.limitations: 该研究仅在模拟环境中进行(未使用真实量子硬件),且论文仅提供抽象层面的细节,限制了对实际应用性的评估 (F5)。

papers.title: Hantavirus Transmission Dynamics in the United States: Reservoir Ecology, Environmental and Social Drivers, and Public Health Implications
papers.abstract: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) is a rare but severe rodent-borne zoonosis. As of the end of 2023, the United States had recorded 890 laboratory-confirmed hantavirus cases since surveillance began in 1993, with 35% case fatality and 94% of cases west of the Mississippi River. This narrative review, searched through November 2026, synthesises epidemiological surveillance, reservoir ecology, ecological niche modelling, social-vulnerability analyses, and climate research to explain where and why Sin Nombre virus (SNV) spills over to people. We integrate evidence that SNV is detected in, and infectious virus isolated from, several rodent species beyond the western deer mouse (Peromyscus sonoriensis, formerly P. maniculatus), though independent maintenance is unproven; niche models linking suitability to arid climates and low-intensity development; the 2025 clusters in New Mexico and California; Seoul virus infections linked to pet rats; and the 2026 Andes virus outbreak on a cruise ship, which renewed attention to person-to-person-transmissible hantaviruses. We separate well-established findings from tentative, correlational inferences about biodiversity, social vulnerability, and climate change, and summarise clinical recognition and management. Priorities include taxonomy-aware rodent surveillance, integrated One Health forecasting, diagnosis and referral to centres offering extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, and targeted prevention for rural, Indigenous, and occupationally exposed communities.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 美国传播动力学:储宿主生态、环境与社会驱动因素及公共卫生影响

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒肺综合征 (HPS) 是一种罕见但严重的啮齿动物传播的人畜共患病,致死率高。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述整合监测、储宿主生态、生态位建模、社会脆弱性和气候研究,以阐明Sin Nombre病毒的跨种传播。
analysis_zh.gaps: 除西部鹿鼠外,SNV在其他啮齿动物种群中的独立维持尚未得到证实,且许多生态和社会关联仍仅为相关性。
analysis_zh.future_research: 优先事项包括基于分类学的啮齿动物监测、One Health 预测、通过 ECMO 转诊提升诊断、以及针对农村、原住民和职业暴露人群的精准防控。

Hantavirus Infection: A Comprehensive Review of Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Prevention Sowmya Santhanam and Sharanya Krishnakumar* Department of Microbiology, Sree Balaji Medical College and Hospital, Bharath Institute of Higher Education and Research, Chennai-600044, Tamil Nadu, India Received: July 27, 2026 / Accepted: August 28, 2026 / Published: November 24, 2026 Introduction Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose a sub- stantial challenge to global public health, particularly when ecological, climatic, and socioeconomic changes alter the interactions between humans, animals, and their environments. Urbanization, climate variability, deforestation, land-use change, and increasing human– animal contact can modify rodent population dynamics and expand opportunities for zoonotic transmission. However, the occurrence of hantavirus infection cannot be attributed to any single environmental factor; rather, it reflects the complex interaction between reservoir ecology, viral characteristics, human behavior, and envi- Hantavirus infection is a globally important zoonosis caused by viruses of the family Hantaviridae, maintained predominantly in rodent reservoirs and transmitted to humans mainly through exposure to contaminated excreta. Ecological disruption, climate variability, deforestation, agricultural expansion, urbanization, and increasing human–animal interactions can modify reservoir dynamics and create opportunities for zoonotic spillover. Depending on the infecting virus, disease ranges from hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) to severe hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS). Disease severity is primarily associated with endothelial dysfunction, increased vascular permeability, immune dysregulation, and cytokine-mediated inflammation. Diagnosis remains challenging because early manifestations are nonspecific and overlap with other endemic febrile illnesses. Serological methods, particularly enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays, remain central to routine diagnosis, while RT-qPCR provides valuable early-phase detection. Emerging approaches, including RT-LAMP, digital PCR, next-generation sequencing, metagenomic sequencing, and CRISPR-based assays, offer opportunities for rapid detection and genomic characterization, although cost, infrastructure, standardization, and clinical validation remain limitations. Treatment is predominantly supportive, with ribavirin showing potential benefit when administered early in selected HFRS cases, while favipiravir, neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed therapies remain investigational. Vaccine development using inactivated, DNA, viral-vector, and mRNA platforms has progressed, but broad and durable protection remains an unmet need. This review critically examines epidemiology, reservoir ecology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnostic advances, therapeutic strategies, vaccine development, prevention, and One Health surveillance. Emphasis is placed on affordable diagnostics, genomic surveillance, early risk prediction, and scalable preventive strategies to strengthen preparedness and reduce the global burden of hantavirus disease. Biotechnol. Lett. 2026 | Vol. 54 ronmental conditions [1]. This complexity makes predic- tion and prevention of hantavirus outbreaks particularly challenging. Hantaviruses are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae. They are maintained predominantly in specific rodent and other small-mammal reservoirs, with individual virus–host associations contributing to distinct geographic and clinical patterns. Human infection generally occurs following inhalation or other exposure to virus-containing rodent excreta or contaminated environmental materials [2]. Although human-to-human transmission is uncommon for most hantaviruses, the ability of these viruses to produce severe disease follow- ing relatively infrequent zoonotic spillover makes them an important public health concern. Thus, the epidemio- logical significance of hantaviruses is determined not only by their geographic distribution but also by the ecological conditions that bring infected reservoirs and susceptible human populations into contact [3]. The clinical importance of hantaviruses became apparent with the recognition of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), historically described as Korean hemorrhagic fever, and the subsequent isolation of Han- taan virus in 1978. The discovery of Sin Nombre virus during the 1993 outbreak in the Four Corners region of the United States further expanded the clinical spectrum of hantavirus disease and established hantavirus cardio- pulmonary syndrome (HCPS) as a severe respiratory manifestation associated with high mortality. These discoveries demonstrated that hantavirus disease is not a single clinical entity but a spectrum of syndromes influenced by viral genotype, reservoir host, geographic distribution, and host response. Despite considerable advances in molecular epidemiology, serological diagnosis, molecular detection, genomic sequencing, and supportive clinical management, important challenges remain unresolved [4]. Early diagnosis is complicated by non- specific initial clinical manifestations and the narrow window during which viral RNA may be detectable, whereas serological assays may be influenced by assay design, antigen selection, and the timing of antibody development. Similarly, advanced approaches such as digital PCR, metagenomic next-generation sequencing, and CRISPR-based diagnostics offer potential advantages but remain constrained by cost, infrastructure, technical expertise, assay standardization, and limited clinical validation. Consequently, the most technologically advanced diagnostic approach is not necessarily the most appropriate for routine use, particularly in resource- limited endemic settings [5]. Therapeutic options also remain limited. Management continues to rely predomi- nantly on early recognition, intensive supportive care, and organ-specific management, while antiviral agents, monoclonal antibodies, and host-directed therapies remain at different stages of investigation. Likewise, the development of broadly protective vaccines is complicated by the genetic and antigenic diversity of hantaviruses and their geographically restricted reservoir associations. These limitations highlight an important gap between technological progress and its translation into accessible clinical and public-health interventions [6]. Against this background, an updated assessment of hantavirus infection should extend beyond a description of established knowledge. A critical evaluation is needed to compare diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, identify limitations in current evidence, examine the feasibility of emerging technologies, and define priorities for sur- veillance, prevention, and vaccine development. This review therefore examines the current understanding of hantavirus virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, laboratory diagnosis, therapeutic strate- gies, prevention, and One Health surveillance, while critically considering unresolved questions, implementa- tion barriers, and future research priorities [7]. Virology Hantaviruses are enveloped, spherical viruses belong- ing to the family Hantaviridae, with virions measuring approximately 80–120 nm in diameter. The viral envelope is derived from the host-cell membrane and contains two surface glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which mediate receptor interaction, cellular attachment, membrane fusion, and viral entry. The genome comprises three segments of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA: the Large (L) segment, which encodes the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) responsible for viral transcription and replication; the Medium (M) segment, which encodes the precursor of the envelope glycoproteins Gn and Gc; and the Small (S) segment, which encodes the nucleocapsid (N) protein [8]. The N protein is involved not only in encapsidation of the viral genome but also in viral replica- tion, assembly, and modulation of host-cell responses. Hantaviruses exhibit considerable genetic and ecological Microbiol. Biotechnol. Lett. 2026 | Vol. 54 3 diversity, with distinct virus-reservoir associations con- tributing to differences in geographic distribution, epide- miology, and clinical disease. Traditionally, hantaviruses associated with HFRS in Asia and Europe have been referred to as Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan virus (HTNV), Seoul virus (SEOV), Puumala virus (PUUV), and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV), whereas viruses associated predominantly with HCPS in the Americas have been classified as New World hantaviruses, including Sin Nombre virus (SNV), Andes virus (ANDV), Laguna Negra virus, and Black Creek Canal virus. Although this geographical classification remains useful from a clinical and epidemiological perspective, it rep- resents a broad framework rather than a strict biologi- cal division, as hantavirus diversity is closely linked to specific reservoir hosts and evolutionary relationships [9]. The relationship between viral genotype, reservoir host, and clinical phenotype is particularly important in understanding disease severity. Old World hantaviruses are predominantly associated with HFRS, whereas several New World hantaviruses are associated with HCPS, characterized by pulmonary capillary leakage, acute respiratory deterioration, and substantial mortality [10]. However, clinical outcome is not determined solely by viral classification and is also influenced by host immune responses, viral factors, and the timing and quality of clinical management. Andes virus is of particular epidemiological interest because person-to-person trans- mission has been well documented, primarily among close contacts in South America, distinguishing it from the transmission patterns observed with most other pathogenic hantaviruses [11]. This observation high- lights the importance of considering virus-specific trans- mission characteristics when developing surveillance, infection-control, and outbreak-response strategies. Epidemiology, Reservoirs, and Transmission Hantavirus epidemiology is closely linked to the dis- tribution and ecology of its small-mammal reservoirs. Although individual hantaviruses generally show strong virus–host associations, the presence of a reservoir species alone does not necessarily result in human disease. Transmission depends on reservoir abundance and infection prevalence, environmental conditions, human behavior, and the frequency of contact between infected animals and susceptible populations. HFRS is predominantly reported in Asia and Europe, with China accounting for a substantial proportion of reported cases, while Puumala virus is the major cause of nephropathia epidemica in Europe. In the Americas, hantavirus infec- tion is primarily associated with HCPS, which generally has a more severe clinical course and higher case-fatality than HFRS [12]. However, regional differences in reported incidence and mortality may reflect not only viral characteristics but also variations in surveillance, diagnostic capacity, early recognition, and access to intensive care. This highlights the importance of inter- preting epidemiological estimates within their healthcare and surveillance context. Important reservoir associations include Apodemus agrarius with Hantaan virus, Myodes glareolus with Puumala virus, Peromyscus maniculatus with Sin Nombre virus, and Sigmodon hispidus with Black Creek Canal virus [13]. These associations con- tribute to the characteristic geographic distribution of hantaviruses, while changes in reservoir population density, habitat, and distribution can influence the temporal and spatial risk of human infection. Human infection most commonly follows inhalation of aerosolized particles contaminated with rodent urine, feces, saliva, or nesting materials. Direct contact with contaminated materials and, less frequently, rodent bites may also result in transmission. Occupational and recreational activities—including agriculture, forestry, military activities, cleaning rodent-infested buildings, camping, and other outdoor exposures—can increase the likeli- hood of contact with infected rodents [14]. Environmental and climatic factors may further modify transmission by influencing rodent abundance and food availability. However, these relationships vary geographically, mak- ing climate alone insufficient for reliable outbreak predic- tion. Integrating environmental monitoring with rodent surveillance and human epidemiological data may provide a more informative assessment of transmission risk. Andes virus is an important exception to the pre- dominantly zoonotic transmission pattern, as person-to- person transmission has been documented, particularly following prolonged and close contact [15]. This virus- specific characteristic has implications for outbreak investigation and infection-control measures and should not be generalized to other hantaviruses. Although hantavirus antibodies have been detected in several domestic and wild animals, serological evidence alone does not establish reservoir competence. Rodents there- fore remain the principal recognized reservoirs of medically 4 Microbiol. Biotechnol. Lett. 2026 | Vol. 54 important hantaviruses. Overall, hantavirus trans- mission is best understood through a reservoir–virus– environment–human framework, supporting the need for integrated One Health surveillance that combines rodent ecology, environmental monitoring, molecular epidemiology, and human disease surveillance [16]. Pathogenesis and Clinical Manifestations The hallmark of hantavirus disease is increased vascular permeability resulting primarily from endothelial dysfunction rather than extensive direct cytopathic injury. Following exposure to virus-contaminated rodent excreta, hantaviruses infect endothelial and immune cells, including macrophages and dendritic cells. Viral entry involves interactions with cellular receptors, including β3 integrins expressed on endothelial cells. Viral replication and the subsequent interaction between infected cells and the host immune system initiate a complex inflammatory response involving cytokines, chemokines, complement activation, and cellular immune mechanisms [17]. Rather than being explained by viral replication alone, vascular leakage appears to result from the combined effects of altered endothelial-cell function and an exaggerated host immune response. Increased levels of inflammatory mediators, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-1β (IL- 1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ), have been associated with endothelial activation and increased vascular permeability. Complement activation and cytotoxic T-cell responses may further influence disease progression. Although cellular immunity is important for controlling viral infection, an excessive or dysregulated immune response may contribute to endo- thelial dysfunction and tissue injury [18]. Thus, disease severity is likely determined by the interaction between viral characteristics, host immune responses, and the extent of endothelial barrier disruption rather than by direct viral cytotoxicity alone. The resulting capillary-leak syndrome provides a com- mon pathological basis for both hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), although the predominant organ involvement and clinical severity differ between these syndromes. HFRS is mainly associated with Old World hantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Its clinical course is traditionally described in febrile, hypotensive, oliguric, diuretic, and convalescent phases, although these phases may overlap and are not uniformly observed in every patient [19]. The febrile phase typically presents with acute fever, severe headache, myalgia, malaise, nausea, vomiting, and occasionally visual disturbances. Progression to the hypotensive phase reflects increasing vascular permeability and may result in plasma leakage, hypotension, tachycardia, and circulatory shock. The subsequent oliguric phase is characterized by acute kidney injury, reduced urine output, proteinuria, hematuria, azotemia, and electrolyte disturbances. Recovery of renal function is followed by a diuretic phase, during which marked polyuria may produce significant fluid and electrolyte losses. The convalescent phase is charac- terized by gradual recovery, although fatigue and reduced physical capacity may persist for weeks or longer. Importantly, the clinical spectrum of HFRS is broad, ranging from the relatively mild nephropathia epidemica associated with Puumala virus to severe disease caused by Hantaan and Dobrava-Belgrade viruses [20]. This variation indicates that clinical outcome is influenced not only by the presence of hantavirus infection but also by virus-specific and host-related factors. HCPS is predominantly associated with New World hantaviruses, particularly Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. analysis.background: The review is prompted by the rising threat of hantavirus zoonoses amid ecological, climatic, and socioeconomic changes that increase human‑rodent contact.
analysis.main_directions: It surveys reservoir ecology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical spectra (HFRS and HCPS), diagnostic advances, therapeutic options, vaccine development, and One‑Health surveillance strategies.
analysis.current_state: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne RNA viruses causing a spectrum of disease; serology (ELISA) and RT‑qPCR are the mainstays of diagnosis, supportive care is standard treatment, ribavirin shows limited benefit, and several vaccine platforms are in development but lack broad, durable protection.
analysis.gaps: Key gaps include incomplete understanding of environmental drivers, early‑phase diagnostic windows, high cost and limited validation of advanced assays, paucity of effective antivirals or monoclonal antibodies, and difficulty achieving cross‑protective vaccines.
analysis.future_research: Priorities are affordable point‑of‑care diagnostics, genomic surveillance for risk prediction, standardization of novel molecular tests, clinical trials of antivirals and monoclonal antibodies, and development of broadly protective, scalable vaccines within a One‑Health framework.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The review is prompted by the rising threat of hantavirus zoonoses amid ecological, climatic, and socioeconomic changes that increase human‑rodent contact. Main directions: It surveys reservoir ecology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical spectra (HFRS and HCPS), diagnostic advances, therapeutic options, vaccine development, and One‑Health surveillance strategies. Current state: Hantaviruses are rodent‑borne RNA viruses causing a spectrum of disease; serology (ELISA) and RT‑qPCR are the mainstays of diagnosis, supportive care is standard treatment, ribavirin shows limited benefit, and several vaccine platforms are in development but lack broad, durable protection. Gaps: Key gaps include incomplete understanding of environmental drivers, early‑phase diagnostic windows, high cost and limited validation of advanced assays, paucity of effective antivirals or monoclonal antibodies, and difficulty achieving cross‑protective vaccines. Future research: Priorities are affordable point‑of‑care diagnostics, genomic surveillance for risk prediction, standardization of novel molecular tests, clinical trials of antivirals and monoclonal antibodies, and development of broadly protective, scalable vaccines within a One‑Health framework.

analysis_zh.background: 由于生态、气候和社会经济变化导致人类与鼠类接触增加,汉坦病毒 人畜共患病威胁上升,促使开展本综述。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 综述内容包括宿主生态、流行病学、致病机制、临床表现(肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征)、诊断进展、治疗方案、疫苗研发以及 One‐Health 监测策略。
analysis_zh.current_state: 汉坦病毒es 是鼠源性 RNA 病毒,可导致多种疾病;血清学(ELISA)和 RT‐qPCR 是诊断的主要手段,支持治疗是标准治疗,利巴韦林疗效有限,多个疫苗平台正在研发中,但缺乏广泛且持久的保护。
analysis_zh.gaps: 主要不足包括对环境驱动因素认识不完整、早期诊断窗口缺乏、高级检测成本高且验证有限、缺乏有效的抗病毒药物或单克隆抗体,以及实现交叉保护疫苗的困难。
analysis_zh.future_research: 优先事项包括经济可及的现场诊断、用于风险预测的基因组监测、新型分子检测的标准化、抗病毒药物和单克隆抗体的临床试验,以及在 One‐Health 框架下研发广谱、可规模化的疫苗。

papers.title: Hantavirus Infections: Virology, Pathogenesis, Clinical Spectrum, and Emerging Therapeutic Frontiers
papers.abstract: Abstract Hantaviruses are rodent-borne zoonotic viruses that cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in Eurasia and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) in the Americas. Despite advances in hantavirus biology and clinical management, no universally approved antiviral therapy exists, and severe HPS remains associated with high mortality. This review summarizes the current understanding of hantavirus virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention, with emphasis on emerging therapeutic strategies. Hantavirus disease is characterized by profound vascular permeability despite limited direct cytopathic injury. Increasing evidence implicates immune-mediated endothelial dysfunction involving β3 integrins, CD8+ T-cell responses, angiopoietin/Tie2 dysregulation, vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, and neutrophil extracellular traps, thereby providing potential targets for antiviral and host-directed therapies. Clinical management remains predominantly supportive. Intravenous ribavirin may benefit patients when administered early in HFRS but has not demonstrated efficacy in established HPS. Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) has emerged as an important rescue therapy for severe HPS with cardiopulmonary collapse. Experimental approaches include favipiravir, direct-acting antivirals, convalescent plasma, broadly neutralizing monoclonal antibodies, viral entry and fusion inhibitors, and strategies targeting pathological host responses. Next-generation vaccine platforms, including DNA vaccines, virus-like particle, and structure-guided subunit vaccines, are under investigation. Integrating structural virology, antiviral discovery, immunology, genomic surveillance, and One Health approaches will be essential for developing effective therapeutic strategies.

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒 感染:病毒学、发病机制、临床范围及新兴治疗前沿

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒es 是啮齿动物传播的动物源性病毒,可导致欧亚地区的 肾综合征出血热 以及美洲的 汉坦病毒肺综合征。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 新兴的治疗研究聚焦于免疫介导的内皮功能障碍通路,包括 β3 整合素、CD8+ T细胞应答、血管生成素/Tie2、VEGF 信号通路以及中性粒细胞胞外陷阱。
analysis_zh.current_state: 该疾病特征为血管通透性显著升高,尽管直接细胞毒性损伤有限,临床治疗仍主要为支持性护理。
analysis_zh.gaps: 目前尚无全球统一批准的抗病毒疗法,且重症 HPS 仍具有高死亡率,凸显治疗空白。
analysis_zh.future_research: 建议整合结构病毒学、抗病毒药物发现、免疫学、基因组监测以及 One Health 方法,以研发有效的抗病毒药物、单克隆抗体和下一代疫苗。

papers.title: Immunoinformatics based design and evaluation of a multi-epitope vaccine candidate targeting the envelopment polyprotein of Andes orthohantavirus.
papers.abstract: Andes Orthohantavirus is known to be the etiological agent for hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which is a highly dangerous disease with a very high death rate. There is no vaccine available to date to protect against this disease. This project aimed to develop a multi-epitope vaccine for Andes Orthohantavirus using immunoinformatics. Epitopes of CTL, HTL, and B cell types were predicted for the shortlisted Glycoprotein precursor after testing antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, and subcellular location. The chosen epitopes were combined using appropriate linkers and β-defensin as an adjuvant to create a multi-epitope vaccine. The final vaccine construct had a length of 296 amino acids and showed excellent antigenicity (0.7297), non-allergenicity, structural stability, and solubility properties. The structure of the vaccine construct showed that 94.6% of residues lie in the preferred areas of the Ramachandran plot, thus ensuring good stereochemistry. Molecular docking and normal mode analysis results confirmed the stable binding of the vaccine construct to TLR-3 receptors. At the same time, immune simulation revealed a fast degradation of antigens, production of antibodies, memory B-cells, and cytokines. In silico cloning integrated the codon-optimized gene with a CAI value of 0.97 and a GC percentage of 49.77% into the plasmid vector pET-28a(+). The designed multi-epitope vaccine displayed good predicted immunogenicity, structure, and expression properties that made it suitable to be used as a potential vaccine candidate against Andes Orthohantavirus infection. Further experimental validation is needed to assess its safety and effectiveness.

analysis.background: Andes orthohantavirus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, a highly dangerous disease with very high death rate, and no vaccine is currently available.
analysis.methods: Immunoinformatics was used to predict CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes from the glycoprotein precursor, which were linked with appropriate linkers and β‑defensin adjuvant to build a 296‑aa construct; antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, subcellular location, structural stability, Ramachandran plot, molecular docking to TLR‑3, normal‑mode analysis, immune simulation, and codon‑optimized in‑silico cloning were performed.
analysis.results: The vaccine construct showed antigenicity 0.7297, non‑allergenicity, 94.6 % residues in favored Ramachandran regions, stable binding to TLR‑3, simulated rapid antigen degradation with antibody, memory B‑cell and cytokine production, and a codon‑adaptation index of 0.97 with 49.77 % GC content.
analysis.contribution: The work presents a computationally validated multi‑epitope vaccine candidate for Andes orthohantavirus, offering a basis for further experimental development.
analysis.limitations: All findings are based on in‑silico analyses; experimental validation of safety and efficacy is needed and only an abstract is available.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Andes orthohantavirus causes hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome with high mortality and no vaccine exists. Methods: Using immunoinformatics, CTL, HTL, and B‑cell epitopes from the glycoprotein precursor were selected, linked with β‑defensin adjuvant, and assembled into a 296‑aa construct; antigenicity, allergenicity, toxicity, subcellular location, structural stability, Ramachandran analysis, molecular docking to TLR‑3, normal‑mode analysis, immune‑simulation, and codon‑optimized in‑silico cloning were performed. Results: The construct showed antigenicity 0.7297, non‑allergenic, 94.6 % residues in favored Ramachandran regions, stable TLR‑3 binding, simulated rapid antigen degradation with antibody, memory B‑cell and cytokine responses, and a CAI of 0.97 with 49.77 % GC. Contribution: The study provides a computationally validated multi‑epitope vaccine candidate for Andes orthohantavirus, supporting further experimental development. Limitations: Findings are based solely on in‑silico analyses; experimental validation of safety and efficacy is required and only an abstract is available.

papers.title: Hantaviruses Through the Lens of Intrinsic Disorder: Structural Plasticity, Pathogenesis, and Therapeutic Opportunities
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are globally distributed zoonotic pathogens responsible for two major clinical syndromes, hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), both associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Despite encoding only a limited repertoire of structural proteins, hantaviruses efficiently manipulate host cellular machinery through highly multifunctional viral proteins. Increasing evidence indicates that intrinsic protein disorder plays a central role in enabling this functional versatility. This review integrates current knowledge on hantavirus epidemiology, transmission dynamics, genome organization, pathophysiology, and therapeutic development while highlighting the emerging importance of intrinsically disordered protein regions in viral biology. Bioinformatic analyses demonstrate that all major hantavirus proteins, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L), envelope glycoprotein precursor (Gn/Gc), and nucleocapsid protein (N) contain flexible or intrinsically disordered regions that facilitate diverse molecular interactions. These structurally dynamic regions contribute to viral RNA encapsulation, replication, receptor recognition, membrane fusion, immune evasion, virion assembly, and modulation of host antiviral responses. The remarkable structural plasticity of hantavirus proteins provides a mechanistic explanation for their multifunctionality and distinct pathogenic manifestations observed between Old World and New World hantaviruses. Furthermore, intrinsic disorder represents a promising yet underexplored avenue for antiviral intervention, complementing current approaches based on antivirals, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, and host-directed therapies. Advances in artificial intelligence-driven structural prediction and disorder analysis are rapidly expanding our understanding of these dynamic proteins and may accelerate the identification of novel therapeutic targets. Collectively, this review emphasizes that intrinsic disorder is not merely a structural characteristic of hantavirus proteins but a fundamental determinant of viral adaptability, pathogenicity, and evolutionary success, offering new perspectives for future mechanistic studies and rational antiviral design.

papers.title: Strengthening readiness for emerging infectious diseases in Somalia through hantavirus preparedness
papers.abstract: Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose substantial threats to global public health security, with low- and middle-income countries bearing a disproportionate burden of vulnerability. In May 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) convened a joint technical briefing (webinar) on hantavirus preparedness, underscoring the importance of proactive readiness for this and other zoonotic threats across the African continent. While no hantavirus outbreak and no direct evidence of human hantavirus circulation have been reported in Somalia, this briefing presents a timely opportunity to critically examine Somalia’s capacity to detect and respond to emerging infectious diseases more broadly. This commentary evaluates Somalia’s current public health infrastructure against the key preparedness domains highlighted in the WHO–Africa CDC briefing including surveillance, laboratory diagnostics, risk communication, and One Health coordination and identifies critical gaps that require urgent policy attention. Drawing on published evidence and international frameworks, we offer context-specific recommendations to strengthen Somalia’s health security architecture before a crisis emerges. Proactive investment in preparedness is both a moral imperative and a strategic necessity for a country at the intersection of complex humanitarian conditions and persistent epidemic risk.

Abstract Emerging infectious diseases continue to pose substantial threats to global public health security, with low- and middle-income countries bearing a disproportionate burden of vulnerability. In May 2026, the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) convened a joint technical briefing (webinar) on hantavirus preparedness, underscoring the importance of proactive readiness for this and other zoonotic threats across the African continent. While no hantavirus outbreak and no direct evidence of human hantavirus circulation have been reported in Somalia, this briefing presents a timely opportunity to critically examine Somalia’s capacity to detect and respond to emerging infectious diseases more broadly. This commentary evaluates Somalia’s current public health infrastructure against the key preparedness domains highlighted in the WHO–Africa CDC briefing including surveillance, laboratory diagnostics, risk communication, and One Health coordination and identifies critical gaps that require urgent policy attention. Drawing on published evidence and international frameworks, we offer context-specific recommendations to strengthen Somalia’s health security architecture before a crisis emerges. Proactive investment in preparedness is both a moral imperative and a strategic necessity for a country at the intersection of complex humanitarian conditions and persistent epidemic risk. 1 Introduction Emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases represent one of the most consequential threats to global public health in the 21st century.Diseases of zoonotic origin those trans­ mitted from animals to humans account for approximately 60% of known human infec­ tious diseases androughly 75% of emerging pathogens identified over recent decades [1]. The COVID-19 pandemic, alongside recurrent outbreaks of Ebola, Marburg, and mpox, has exposed the catastrophic cost of inadequate preparedness, particularly in low-resource settings where health systemcapacity is structurally constrained [2].Low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) face a dual challenge: they carry the highest bur­ den ofinfectious disease while simultaneously confronting the most severe deficits in the Page 2 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 systems required to detect and respond to emerging threats.Sub-Saharan Africa, and the Horn of Africa in particular, remains among the most vulnerable regions in the world to pandemic-scale events,owing to ecological conditions favorable to zoonotic spillover, high population density in informal settlements, limited diagnosticinfrastructure, and fragmented health governance [3].Against this backdrop, the joint technical briefing (webinar) convened by the WorldHealth Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) in May 2026on hantavirus preparedness represents a significant institutional signal. Prompted by WHO and Africa CDC’s response to emerging hantaviruscases [4], the briefing was designed to strengthen proactive readiness across the region, encouraging member states across the Africancontinent to assess their surveillance systems, laboratory capacities, and One Health coordination mechanisms in anticipation of potentialzoonotic threats [5]. This forward-looking approach aligns with the principles embedded in the International Health Regulations (2005) andthe Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction, both of which emphasize preparedness as the cornerstone of resilient health systems [6].This commentary uses the WHO–Africa CDC hantavirus technical briefing as an analytical lens through which to examine Somalia’spreparedness for emerging infectious diseases. We do not assert that Somalia faces an imminent hantavirus threat; rather, we argue that thepreparedness domains highlighted in the briefing surveillance, diagnostics, risk communication, and multisectoral coordination reflectuniversal gaps in Somalia’s health security infrastructure that merit urgent and sustained policy attention. 2 Why hantavirus preparedness matters globally and regionally Hantaviruses are RNA viruses belonging to the family Hantaviridae, transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolscontaminated with the excreta of infected rodents [7]. They cause two serious clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome(HFRS), which is prevalent in Europe and Asia, and hantavirus car­ diopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), which predominates in the Americas. Casefatality rates range from less than 1% for some HFRS-causing strains to over 30% for certain HCPS-causing strains [7]. Critically, no licensedvaccine or specific antiviral treatment is currently available, making prevention, early detection, and supportive care the prin­ cipal public healthtools. The continued global relevance of hantavirus was underscored in May 2026, when WHO reported responding to human hantavirus caseslinked to a cruise ship [4].Evidence of hantavirus-seropositive rodents has been documented in multiple African countries, including in sub-Saharan Africa, raising the possibility, at a regional and ecological level, of undetected human cases on the continent [8]. Such rodentseroprevalence data indicate biological plausibility across parts of Africa; they are not, however, direct evidence of hantavirus circulation inany specific country, includ­ ing Somalia [8]. The widespread presence of reservoir rodent species (particularly Muri­ nae and Cricetidae),combined with limited diagnostic capacity to distinguish hantavirus from other febrile illnesses such as malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, andviral hemorrhagic fevers, means that hantavirus infections in Africa may be significantly underdiagnosed and underreported [8].The globalpublic health community has increasingly recognized that the absence of confirmed cases does not imply the absence of risk lessons rein­ forcedby repeated experiences with emerging pathogens. The WHO–Africa CDC brief­ ing reflects this paradigm shift: preparedness must precededetection. For African health Page 3 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 systems, this requires investment in syndromic surveillance, rodent reservoir monitor­ ing, differential diagnosticcapacity, and cross-sectoral preparedness planning before an outbreak demands emergency mobilization. 3 Relevance to Somalia Somalia presents a complex and challenging public health environment shaped by three decades of conflict, recurrent humanitarian crises, andfragmented governance. Despite recent political stabilization efforts and incremental progress in health system recon­ struction, the FederalGovernment of Somalia’s capacity to prevent, detect, and respond to infectious disease outbreaks remains severely constrained [9]. Thecountry has one of the lowest health expenditure levels in the world, inadequate health workforce density, and a healthcare infrastructure thatwas severely disrupted during the civil conflict period and remains unevenly distributed across regions [10].Somalia’s epidemiological pro­ fileis dominated by endemic and epidemic-prone diseases, including cholera, measles, acute watery diarrhea, polio, and malaria. In 2022 and2023, the country simultaneously managed a severe drought-driven humanitarian emergency, widespread displacement of over 3.8 millioninternally displaced persons (IDPs), and multiple concurrent disease outbreaks [11]. The convergence of malnutrition, poor sanitation,overcrowded displace­ ment settlements, and limited access to healthcare creates conditions highly condu­ cive to infectious disease transmissionand amplification.While hantavirus has not been reported in Somalia, the ecological and socioeconomic conditions that favor zoonotic­ spillover are present. Rodent infestation is a recognized problem in IDP settlements and urban areas [12]. Human–animal interfaces arefrequent in a predominantly pastoralist society, and exposure to rodent reservoirs in agricultural and peri-urban environments is common.Crucially, the diagnostic tools and clinical awareness needed to identify hantavirus, or other emerging zoonotic diseases, remain very limitedwithin Somalia’s current health system capacity. It should be emphasized, however, that no direct evi­ dence of hantavirus circulation in Somaliacurrently exists; the concern is one of biologi­ cal plausibility and general preparedness rather than documented or imminent human risk. Inprinciple, an emerging infectious disease could circulate for a period before iden­ tification—the broad scenario that the WHO–Africa CDCbriefing urges countries to guard against. 4 Key messages from the WHO–Africa CDC technical briefing As a webinar, this briefing served as a timely prompt rather than a formally published technical document, and no recording or presentationmaterials from it are publicly available; the preparedness principles it reiterated are themselves established in verifi­ able international guidance, to which the messages below are anchored in particular the International Health Regulations (2005) [6], the One Health Joint Plan of Action [13], and established WHO and Africa CDC preparedness and surveillance frameworks [14,15]. 4.1 Surveillance systems and early warning The technical briefing emphasized the centrality of robust surveillance systems to early detection of emerging zoonotic threats. Effectivesurveillance requires functional dis­ ease reporting networks, standardized case definitions, real-time data management, and Page 4 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 integrationbetween human, animal, and environmental health surveillance streams [5]. Event-based surveillance—the systematic monitoring ofinformal reports and commu­ nity signals is particularly valuable in settings where laboratory-confirmed case identi­ fication is delayed. 4.2 Laboratory preparedness and diagnostics A core message of the briefing was that laboratory capacity for emerging pathogen diag­ nostics is foundational to preparedness. This includesaccess to biosafety level-2 and level-3 facilities, availability of validated diagnostic assays (including serological and molecular tests foremerging viruses), specimen referral networks, and quality-assured laboratory practices. Without these, even clinically suspicious casescannot be con­ firmed, hampering both outbreak response and epidemiological understanding [5]. 4.3 Risk communication and community engagement The briefing underlined that risk communication and community engagement (RCCE) are not supplementary but integral to preparedness.Effective RCCE enables commu­ nities to recognize and report unusual illness presentations, reduces harmful health- seeking delays, buildstrust between communities and health authorities, and counters misinformation. Importantly, RCCE must be culturally adapted andlinguistically acces­ sible to be effective in diverse community contexts [16]. 4.4 One Health preparedness and multisectoral coordination Perhaps the most structurally significant message of the briefing was its emphasis on One Health an integrative approach recognizing theinterdependence of human, ani­ mal, and environmental health. For zoonotic diseases such as hantavirus, preparedness requires activecoordination between ministries of health, livestock, environment, and agriculture; engagement with veterinary and wildlife authorities; andjoint surveillance and response planning [5, 13]. Siloed sectoral approaches are fundamentally insufficient for managing the complexdynamics of zoonotic disease emergence. 5 Preparedness gaps and risks in Somalia 5.1 Surveillance limitations Somalia’s disease surveillance infrastructure is fragmented and heavily dependent on external humanitarian partners for operationalcontinuity. The Integrated Disease Sur­ veillance and Response (IDSR) framework, endorsed by the African Union and WHO, has beenpartially implemented in Somalia but lacks consistent application across all federal member states [9]. Data completeness, timeliness ofreporting, and feedback mechanisms remain significant challenges. Syndromic surveillance for febrile hemor­ rhagic illness syndromesremains limited in functionality and geographic coverage, and is inconsistently implemented across federal member states, which isparticularly concern­ ing from an emerging disease preparedness standpoint. 5.2 Laboratory and diagnostic capacity Somalia’s disease surveillance infrastructure is fragmented and heavily dependent on external humanitarian partners for operationalcontinuity. The Integrated Disease Sur­ veillance and Response (IDSR) framework, endorsed by the African Union and WHO, Page 5 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 has beenpartially implemented in Somalia but lacks consistent application across all federal member states [9]. Data completeness, timeliness ofreporting, and feedback mechanisms remain significant challenges. Syndromic surveillance for febrile hemor­ rhagic illness syndromesremains limited in functionality and geographic coverage, and is inconsistently implemented across federal member states, which isparticularly concern­ ing from an emerging disease preparedness standpoint. 5.3 Cross-border health security challenges Somalia shares porous borders with Ethiopia, Kenya, and Djibouti, and significant cross- border movement occurs through pastoralistmigration, livestock trade, and refugee flows. These movement patterns facilitate rapid regional dissemination of infectious dis­ eases, asdemonstrated during cholera and measles outbreaks [11]. Health surveillance at points of entry is limited in coverage and functionality,particularly at land crossings used by pastoralist and informal cross-border movement, and this, together with weak cross-border informationsharing mechanisms, represents meaningful vulnerabilities in regional health security. 5.4 Humanitarian and displacement-related vulnerabilities As of 2023, Somalia hosts one of the largest internally displaced populations in sub- Saharan Africa [11]. IDP settlements are characterizedby overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, poor rodent vector control, and extremely limited access to healthcare. These conditions amplifyboth the risk of zoonotic exposure and the potential for rapid second­ ary transmission of person-to-person pathogens. Humanitarian crises alsodivert gov­ ernment and partner attention and resources away from preparedness activities toward acute response, creating cyclical gaps inreadiness. 5.5 Workforce and infrastructure constraints Somalia faces a severe shortage of trained public health professionals, epidemiologists, laboratory scientists, and infection control specialists.Health worker density is among the lowest globally, and much of the existing health workforce is concentrated in major urban centers,leaving significant coverage gaps in rural and peri-urban areas [10]. The capacity for rapid deployment of field epidemiology teams,outbreak investigation, and case management during novel disease events is correspondingly limited. 6 Policy and public health recommendations The recommendations below follow directly from the gaps identified in Sect.5and are grouped by feasibility. Immediate, feasible actions—achievable within existing part­ nerships and resources—include full operationalization of IDSR with community- and event-based surveillance(6.1, addressing 5.1), strengthened specimen-referral agree­ ments with regional and international reference laboratories (6.3, short-termcomponent, addressing 5.2), scaling Field Epidemiology Training Program cohorts (6.2, address­ ing 5.5), and preparedness-phase riskcommunication (6.6). Longer-term, resource- dependent goals include establishing in-country BSL-2 molecular diagnostic capacity (6.3,medium-term component, addressing 5.2), formalized One Health coordination structures (6.5), and institutionalized cross-border data-sharingand RISLNET participa­ tion (6.4, addressing 5.3). Page 6 of 8 Issack Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1840 6.1 Strengthen early warning and surveillance systems Somalia should prioritize full operationalization of the IDSR framework across all federal member states, with particular attention tostrengthening community-based surveillance, event-based surveillance, and integrated reporting platforms. papers.title_zh: 通过汉坦病毒准备工作加强索马里对新发传染病的应对能力

analysis_zh.background: 新发传染病对低收入和中等收入国家的威胁尤为突出,索马里脆弱的卫生系统进一步加剧了这一风险。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者撰写了评论文章,依据已发表的证据和国际框架,将索马里的公共卫生基础设施与 WHO–非洲 CDC 汉坦病毒 的防备领域进行评估。
analysis_zh.results: 截至目前,索马里未报告 汉坦病毒 疫情或人类传播的直接证据,但分析指出在监测、诊断、风险沟通以及 One Health 协调方面存在关键缺口。

papers.title: Andes Virus Exposure and Nosocomial Transmission Events to Healthcare Personnel: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) is a high-consequence infectious disease with substantial mortality. On 2 May 2026, the World Health Organization reported a multinational ANDV outbreak, raising questions regarding the risk of transmission to healthcare personnel (HCP). METHODS: We performed a systematic review per PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO:CRD420261283806) for studies describing healthcare-associated ANDV exposure or transmission events to HCP. RESULTS: Eight studies reporting on 7 events were included, describing a total of 17 healthcare-associated cases. Overall, 207 individuals were exposed, including 118 HCP, resulting in 8 infections and 4 deaths among HCP. Studies describing HCP infections reported none or inadequate personal protective equipment (PPE) use. CONCLUSIONS: Transmission of ANDV to HCP has been reported in the setting of delayed implementation of transmission-based precautions or breaches in infection control practice. Limitations in published exposure events highlight the need for standardized reporting of exposure events and outcomes as well as infection prevention measures implemented.

Future research: Implement standardized exposure reporting, conduct prospective HCP surveillance, and test PPE and precaution effectiveness.

papers.full_text: 이호왕의 유행성출혈열 연구와 한탄바이러스 발견 Ho Wang Lee’s Research of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever and Discovery of Hantaan Virus 8 조회 3 이용 0 인용 0 참고문헌 키워드 초록 Abstract This paper argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever(EHF) was the result of repeated failures and trials on new objects and new experimental methods. Generally speaking, scientific papers describe the research process as going a straight way leading to the final results. However, researches in the real world are full of trial-and-errors, misunderstandings, and complex interactions among elements in the laboratory. Ho Wang Lee’s research is a good case to show such characteristics of the scientific research.In this paper, Lee’s researches from 1970 to 1980 are examined into three periods. First, from 1970 to 1973, he studied about EHF using wild rats as an experimental object. Wild rats were widely suspected to have the agent of EHF but he failed to get any results. During the second period from 1974 to 1976, he identified an agent of EHF, Korea Antigen, by introducing a new experimental object, the lung of wild rats, and a new method, Fluorescent Antibody Technique. For last 4 years from 1977 to 1980, Lee clarified its physicochemical features. With the results, the Korea Antigen was registered as the agent of EHF, Hantaan Virus in 1980.
